text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

She smiled in a friendly way, but he didn’t respond. She thought for a second he was a statue and wondered why no one else seemed to have seen him yet.
Then his shoulders moved, subtly, in the direction of the couch. It seemed less like an invitation than a challenge.
Mara stopped in the middle of the room and looked around, at the empty chairs and tables, at the wall lined with books. She saw no place that looked more inviting than the couch, but she didn’t want to make him move or turn again if he didn’t want to. So she stood still.
He didn’t look away. She realized that he was going to wait her out, and decided to see who would blink first.
The pause stretched. The sound of voices rose faintly from somewhere outside the building. He leaned back further against the wall, and she could almost feel his muscles stretch and relax.
After what seemed like minutes, she felt a slight sensation in the back of her neck, as though someone were breathing there, or had laid a hand lightly against the nape of her neck.
She turned around, but nobody was there.
“I’m Mara,” she said aloud. “What’s your name?”

segment:
His head tilted a fraction in her direction. His hair fell across his face, and a breeze moved it. For an instant, he looked like someone she knew: an old friend who was dead now.
Then his face came clear again and he blinked. It wasn’t his voice that answered.
“This is Adrian,” Livia said. She came into the room from the hallway and crossed to stand beside Mara, looking at the young man on the couch.
“Adrian,” she said, “this is Mara. He’s been here a few years already, but I thought he was due for some fresh conversation. Do you mind?”
He shrugged again. The motion looked casual, but it felt to Mara as though it carried some significance.
Mara didn’t say anything, but looked at Livia and smiled. She felt as if they were taking the measure of each other, testing boundaries and possibilities.
It wasn’t clear what kind of test Adrian had intended, but he seemed content enough to let Livia step in. He watched them both with his head tilted and his eyes narrowed.

Mara could hear the faint sound of music coming from outside the house. “What is that?” she asked, pointing to the sound.
“The dining hall,” said Livia. “It’s not far away. We all go there to eat.”

Mara had seen a map when she first arrived and remembered the outline of the compound. She felt a surge of curiosity about the rest of the building and looked around for someone else to talk to. But no one else was in the room, and Adrian still watched her silently from his corner of the couch.

Mara walked over to the window and stood looking out at the yard beyond. There was some sort of metal sculpture on the grass, and several chairs and tables. A few people sat around a fire pit. The sky was clear, but a thin cloud covered most of the moon.

segment:
He relaxed at once and pushed himself up on the couch, looking her up and down with interest.

“Adrian,” he said, with a hint of an accent that she couldn’t place. He nodded toward the chair by the couch, but she was still wary.
“Thank you,” she said. “How do you like it here so far?”

She thought his shoulders twitched, just slightly, but the only sign of amusement was in his eyes. The rest of his face remained expressionless. He had a small scar on his lower lip.

“It’s fine,” he said. He crossed one leg and leaned forward with one hand on the armrest, so that one side of his body faced her squarely.

She sat down in the chair he had pointed at and crossed one leg as well, careful to keep her eyes on his.

“And where are you from?” she asked.
“South Africa.”

Mara nodded. She waited for more.

He looked past her, out the window.

“I was interested,” Mara said, “to hear that you were in the program in South Africa.”

She saw him exhale slowly. He put his hand down and looked back at her, unsmiling.
“Were you?” he said.
Mara was not sure how much she wanted to say. She nodded.

He waited for more. She shrugged.

They sat there silently. It seemed as if he was thinking about saying something, but then he decided not to. Instead, he turned back to his original position and closed his eyes. She could see that his body had relaxed again.
“You must have been quite young,” she said after a moment.
His body tensed again, but he didn’t open his eyes.

“Not that it matters.”

She took a deep breath and glanced away, out the window. She hadn’t meant to imply that it was strange that he was still so young. He didn’t say anything.

After another long moment, she said, “Are you going to do the same program here?”
He opened his eyes and turned to look at her.
“No.”

segment:
A faint smile brushed the young man’s lips.
“My name is Jonah,” he replied, his voice soft and smooth as water running over pebbles. “And you’re not in my mind, Mara.”

“I wasn’t asking about that.”
He said nothing more. She waited for a second, then sat down in the chair by the window. It had a good view of the surrounding trees, which were green and lush in the afternoon sun. She thought she saw a deer pass by, but it was gone before she could be sure.
“I don’t think I’ve ever seen you around here,” she said, still watching the woods beyond the window. “Are you new?”
“No,” he replied. “I’ve been here for almost a year now.”

“And what are you doing right now? Or rather, what were you doing?”
He didn’t answer. She looked up, startled, but he was still looking at her. A moment later he spoke, his voice like liquid silk. “I am just reading a book about telepathy,” he said.
“What does it say?” she asked him, curious.
His mouth twisted a little in what seemed to be amusement. “It says that telepathic abilities are developed through meditation,” he replied.

She looked at him again. He had closed his eyes as though to hide something from her; the expression on his face was neutral and unrevealing.
“How do you know about that?” she asked. “Who told you?”
He smiled a little, but did not reply. He was clearly enjoying this conversation very much, she thought, although he seemed not to realize it. She had to admit it was amusing herself; the fact that she couldn’t get any direct information out of him was both intriguing and annoying. It reminded her of trying to talk to her younger brother sometimes, who could be like that too. But somehow this felt different, as though something were missing from his response.

segment:
His expression changed, not quite enough to smile. But he said, “Adrian.”
“Hello.”
“Hi.” He raised his free hand a fraction of an inch in greeting, keeping it close to his chest.
She walked toward him, feeling slightly awkward but unable to find an alternative. The smell of the building, new and neutral and faintly antiseptic, was suddenly strong in her nostrils; he exhaled slightly as he watched her approach, and she could feel his body heat. The sound of feet and voices from outside became louder; a door opened and someone else came in.

As Mara neared the couch, he said, “I think your bag is open,” in the low but clear voice she’d come to expect in this place.
She looked down at her bag. Sure enough, the zipper wasn’t fully closed. She tugged on it and the bag slid open farther, spilling her belongings out. She crouched down to gather them up, her face still turned toward him.
He shifted his position again. He must know that she could see him watching her, and it didn’t seem as if he cared whether he was watched in return. The sense of a breath, or a hand, behind her head was stronger. Her spine tingled.
She zipped her bag closed, then sat back on her heels and looked at him. He was leaning forward now, watching her face closely.
“Are you the same person?” she asked abruptly.
He frowned and tilted his head to one side. “I think so.”
“Does that ever happen?”
“What?”
“Does your body change? Do you have multiple bodies?”
He smiled. “No,” he said.
“Good,” she said, and stood up. She felt her cheeks reddening, but there was nothing to be done about that. “I’m glad.”
His eyes widened slightly. She turned and headed toward the back of the room, away from his gaze, where she sat on the floor against one of the walls and tried to calm her breathing.
Her phone buzzed.

segment:
The man on the couch didn’t respond.
“Adrian.” He had said it so quietly that she didn’t even notice until a moment later. She blinked and turned toward him again, her eyes focusing. He wasn’t looking at her anymore, but at the blank wall beside the couch. She could see a little of his face in profile, an aquiline nose and a high cheekbone.
“So, Adrian,” she said, “do you want to play a game?”

He turned his head back to look at her, one eyebrow quirked up, and she felt as though a small breeze had moved the air between them. It was as though he were saying, Yes, what did you have in mind?
She had no idea what he would be like, or whether he would respond to anything at all, but she had been trained at Fulcrum to expect the unexpected, and to trust her gut instincts when it came to other people’s behavior.
“I don’t know,” she said after a moment. “Let me think.”
She let his image slip from focus. She felt the movement of his breath shift slightly as he settled into his seat, and she imagined a soft whoosh of air coming from his open mouth. He was still there, waiting.

She blinked and turned toward him again, trying to refocus on his face. But it was hard to find the right angle; her eyes kept slipping away.
“Okay,” she said after a moment. “Let’s go with this.”
And as though from nowhere, there were people around her—an invisible crowd that seemed to materialize in response to her words. She turned to see them, but they were like shadows, ghostly and indistinct.
A few of them shifted toward her, but most seemed to be watching something behind her. She turned to follow their gaze and saw the outline of a figure against the far wall of the room. Adrian.
